theme: Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 128 and Psalm 129. These are Songs of Ascents. Psalm 128 describes the blessing of a family that fears the LORD. Psalm 129 remembers a long history of affliction and survival. Read them as the two sides of pilgrim life: peace at home, and enemies on the road.
settingTheScene: These two psalms are placed side by side in the Songs of Ascents. Psalm 128 is a wisdom psalm that was likely sung at weddings and family festivals. Psalm 129 recalls how Israel had been attacked “from my youth” yet never overcome. Together they speak to people who had been through exile and survived: God blesses the faithful, and he preserves his people through persecution.
observation: “Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways!” (128:1).
“You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you” (128:2).
“Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table” (128:3).
“Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD” (128:4).
“The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life!” (128:5).
“Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth” (129:1).
“Yet they have not prevailed against me” (129:2).
“The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked” (129:4).
interpretation:
Psalm 128 is a short portrait of a blessed life. The blessing is not described in terms of wealth or power, but of ordinary things: work that is fruitful, a family that is flourishing, and a table with children around it. The source is “the fear of the LORD,” a reverent trust that shapes daily life. The man who walks in God’s ways finds that his labor is blessed, and his home is a place of joy.

The picture of the fruitful vine and olive shoots is of life and growth. A vine in a home was a sign of abundance. Olive shoots, around a table, were a sign of vitality. The psalm does not promise that every godly person will have a large family or comfortable job. It describes the shape of God’s blessing in the ordinary life of his people, and it places that blessing within the larger blessing of Zion: “May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life! May you see your children’s children!” Personal and communal blessing go together.

Psalm 129 is a contrast. “Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth.” Israel’s history from Egypt on has been one of oppression. “Yet they have not prevailed against me.” It is a statement of survival. Plowmen plowed on my back, and made long their furrows. But the LORD is righteous. He cut the cords of the wicked. And the psalm closes with a curse on those who hate Zion: let them be like grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows, and which no reaper can use. Even in affliction, the people were not destroyed.

Together, these psalms speak to the situation of the exiles. They had survived. They were returning home to rebuild homes and families. The God who had kept them through persecution would bless them in ordinary life.
connection: Matthew 6:33 says to seek first the kingdom of God. Ephesians 5:22-33 and 6:1-4 teach about the family under God. Psalm 1:2-3 describes the blessed person like a tree by the water. Romans 8:35-37 says that in all things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. 2 Corinthians 4:8-9: “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed.” Matthew 16:18: the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church.
application:
Give thanks for ordinary blessings: your work, your table, your family or friends. Name them to God.

Pray for the families in your church to flourish in the fear of the LORD.

Remember the afflictions you have survived. Say, “Yet they have not prevailed against me,” as a testimony.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to bless your work and your home.
Thank him that he is righteous and cuts the cords of the wicked.
Bless the families of your church.
